content: The Zika virus has been detected in the serum and saliva of adult men and women, but no studies have explored its presence in sweat. A review identified cases where Zika virus was found in human breast milk. In one case series, the virus was detected in milk samples collected five days after the onset of maternal symptoms, but no infectious virus was found in cell cultures. In other cases, milk samples collected 3–4 days after symptom onset tested positive for Zika virus, and infectious particles were confirmed in cell cultures. However, among three women, no virus was detected in milk samples collected four or more days after symptom onset. The virus was also found in colostrum 14 days after symptom onset and in milk samples 23 and 32 days after onset, with infectious particles confirmed in cell cultures. Another review included nine studies with ten cases of Zika virus infection. Five cases involved infection during pregnancy (via transplacental transmission or at delivery), one case occurred 0–4 days after birth, two cases between 8 weeks and 6 months, and two cases beyond 6 months. In five cases, Zika virus was confirmed in the mothers' breast milk. Two newborns were breastfed from birth, one case avoided breastfeeding, and one case did not specify breastfeeding status. One infant appeared to have been infected just before delivery, with transient Zika virus detection and a mild rash, but no complications were observed at 32 months, and the infant was breastfed for two months. In two cases, Zika virus was detected in maternal urine but not in breast milk, and one infant was exclusively breastfed for five months without symptoms. In two other cases, Zika virus was detected in maternal serum, with one case showing infectious particles in breast milk cell cultures. Breastfeeding was avoided in this case until the maternal rash resolved, and the infant remained asymptomatic. Another mother breastfed during her symptomatic period, and the infant was asymptomatic and tested negative for Zika virus. A systematic review found that three out of seven breastfeeding children from mothers with suspected or confirmed Zika virus infection showed evidence of infection. However, no confirmed Zika virus infections were reported in cohort studies of breastfeeding infants. No adverse outcomes or long-term complications were reported in infants exposed to Zika virus through breastfeeding, and the consequences of infection in infants were generally mild and transient. The mechanism by which Zika virus is present in breast milk but does not infect infants has been explored. A study found that freezing human breast milk inhibited Zika virus infection, while fresh milk did not. Storing milk for two days or using cold storage also inactivated the virus. This antiviral activity is thought to be due to the fat-containing cream fraction of milk, which destroys viral particles. Variability in this activity may be related to differences in milk fat composition among women. The benefits of breastfeeding, even in the context of maternal Zika virus infection, outweigh the potential risks. Breastfeeding provides significant advantages for infant survival, health, and development, as well as maternal health. The evidence suggests that the risk of Zika virus transmission through breastfeeding is very low, and no long-term complications have been documented in infants exposed to the virus through breast milk. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that infants born to mothers with suspected or confirmed Zika virus infection should be breastfed according to standard guidelines. This includes initiating breastfeeding within one hour of birth, exclusive breastfeeding for six months, and continued breastfeeding with complementary foods up to two years or beyond. There is insufficient evidence to make recommendations regarding breastfeeding by women vaccinated against Zika virus, as no vaccine is currently available. The development of a Zika virus vaccine remains a priority, particularly for pregnant women, as even asymptomatic infections can result in congenital Zika syndrome. Inactivated vaccines may be more suitable for women of childbearing age, while live attenuated vaccines could be used for other populations. As of January 2019, several clinical trials were underway to evaluate candidate vaccines, but no vaccine is commercially available. In summary, the benefits of breastfeeding for both infants and mothers far outweigh the potential risks of Zika virus transmission through breast milk. The evidence supports continued breastfeeding in areas of Zika virus transmission, with appropriate guidance and support for mothers.
